newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: France's Giat Industries in new UAE offset deal.
newsitem.headline: France's Giat Industries in new UAE offset deal.

text.p: France's Giat Industries, as part of its obligation to offset a $3.62 billion tank deal with the United Arab Emirates, on Monday announced a new investment in an Abu Dhabi-based shipping venture.

The UAE Offsets Group (UOG) and state-owned Giat said at a news conference the company, Combined Cargo UAE, was being incorporated to own and operate vessels and broker cargo and vessels and had an initial paid up capital of $15 million.

The firm, which is already operational, is a joint venture between Giat which holds 25 percent, Norwegian shipping firm Torvald Klaveness Group (24 percent), Abu Dhabi Investment Company (25 percent), Oman and Emirates Investment Holding Company which is a joint venture between the governments of Oman and the UAE (15 percent), and local firm United Technical Services (11 percent).

"It is hoped that with the future expansion of the activities of the company, the dependency on foreign shippers for the transportation of bulk commodities in and out of the Arabian Gulf will be reduced," said the statement.
The venture is one of six offset projects that Giat has launched in the UAE, an oil-rich Gulf Arab state that has emerged as a key customer in the international arms bazaar.

Industry sources say the French arms maker has been struggling to meet its offset obligations since it won a $3.62 billion UAE order in 1993 for Leclerc main battle tanks, making it the biggest offset player in the country.

They say the key question is whether the new project will boost Giat's efforts to meet its offset requirements by its 2003 deadline. So far, it has met 40 percent of its obligation, company officials say.
Combined Cargo UAE's ships will be flagged in Norway and will operate globally, UOG head Amin Badr el-Din told reporters.
Giat Offset's project manager Nasri Tehini said the company was already making profits but he would not disclose how much.
"I reserve an opinion on that, we hope for very good profits," he said. "We are making money now. We have met all our targets so far in our business strategies."
Some Western arms manufacturers say they are entangled in the offset programme's list of conditions and complain of a lack of investment opportunities in the UAE.
The UOG was launched in July 1990 when the UAE activated a plan to buy high-tech weapons worth billions of dollars.
